subject: penguin
reasoning:
I'm planning out a blocky stylized penguin model using the SDK, with a black back, white belly, orange beak and feet, flippers, and eyes, and setting up the necessary imports and helper functions to construct it.

I'm sketching the skeleton: a hips root joint, a spine chain curving upward through several points to the head, and a head joint on top, so the body has a natural upright posture around 0.7 meters tall.

For the body mesh itself, I'm leaning toward sweeping an egg-shaped profile along the spine chain, using a radius function to get the rounded penguin torso shape rather than building explicit loft stations.

For the belly/back coloring, I'll use a paint function that checks the surface normal's z-component to split white belly from black back, giving a stylized penguin coloring without needing smooth blending. For the feet, I'll keep it simple with flat orange extruded shapes attached to the hip joint rather than a full limb rig.

Working out extrude orientation for the feet so the outline lies flat in the forward-sideways plane with thickness along the vertical axis, then sketching a webbed foot outline using forward and sideways coordinates centered appropriately on each side.

Now I'm thinking through the flipper design, treating wings as a bone chain with shoulder, elbow, and wrist joints following a curved path, parented to the spine.

For the flipper's geometry, I'm sweeping a flattened tube along that chain with a radius function that tapers and squashes the shape toward the tip, giving it a paddle-like black-colored appearance consistent with the body's black coloring.

Now I'm working out the spine hierarchy: defining a catmull-spline path from hips through chest to neck as a 3-span chain whose first joint doubles as the root, then attaching a separate head joint to the chain's final joint.

Adjusting the radius profile so the hips sit lower and the body tapers correctly between feet, belly, and neck, then switching to an elliptical cross-section that's wider sideways than front-to-back to give the penguin its characteristic flipper-out shape.

For coloring, I'm defining a paint function that splits the body into black back and white belly based on the surface normal's z-component, and doing something similar for the head to create a dark crown with a lighter front-facing patch resembling a penguin's face.

Now I'm placing the head sphere on its bone and adjusting the vertical position so it sits naturally atop the body without excessive overlap, then moving on to shaping the beak as a small cone-like spike extending from the head.

For the mouth, I'm splitting it into separate upper and lower jaw pieces attached near the head joint, and sketching out the beak's side-profile outline as a thin wedge shape to extrude into a 3D form.

Setting up the jaw joint and positioning the lower beak slightly below the upper one to create a small gap. Now I'm moving on to the eyes, planning a white sphere with a darker pupil for that classic penguin look.

Now I'm working out the flipper chain geometry, placing shoulder, elbow, and hand points on the body surface and parenting the chain to the chest joint. I'm figuring out the sweep profile for the flipper tube so it reads as flat like a real penguin wing rather than round.

I'll settle on tapered circular tubes for the flipper shape, stylized but acceptable. For the tail, I'm adding a small nub using a spike primitive from the hips pointing back and slightly up. Feet will be a simple orange extrude attached at the hip joint, and I'm finalizing the color palette (black, white, orange body tones, black eyes, orange-yellow beak) while considering a subtle chin patch detail but deciding to keep things modest and skip adding ground geometry.

For the belly coloring, I'm writing a paint function that checks the normal and position to decide between white and black, confirming that accessing p.y works based on documented examples, and now moving on to defining the paint logic for the head sphere.

Setting up joints for head and jaw with appropriate parent bones, positions, and directions for later posing, then starting on the spine chain and overall builder structure...

Writing body sweep radius profile...

I'm adjusting hip height to 0.12 so the body's rounded bottom cap meets the feet seamlessly, then starting to sketch out the flipper chains with shoulder, elbow, and hand joints positioned along the sides of the body.

Now I'm defining the sweep radii for the flippers, tapering from wider at the shoulder to narrower at the hand, colored black, and working through the foot placement and outline coordinates relative to the hip bone's orientation.

Shifting to the tail, I'm positioning a spike geometry angled backward and downward from the body base, approximating the direction vector since it may not need to be unit-length. For the beak, I'm extruding a thin three-point outline with a sharp tip, oriented along the head's forward axis with a narrow thickness to keep it proportionate to the face.

Now I'm working out the lower jaw piece similarly, with a separate outline and a joint attaching it to the head so it could later be posed open or closed. I'm checking the vertical placement of both beak halves to make sure there's a small gap between them representing the mouth opening, rather than letting them overlap or float disconnected from the head sphere.

I'm placing the eyes symmetrically on either side of the head using white sphere bases with smaller black pupils, then double-checking the distances from the head center so the eyes sit properly embedded into the head surface rather than floating outside it. I also realize the head coloring needs adjusting so the white eye sclera doesn't disappear against a white face region -- I'm reworking the paint function to make the area around the eyes black so the white eyeballs stand out properly, like a typical penguin face pattern.

For the body, I'm defining the paint logic so the chest stays white within a vertical band while everything else, including the top where wings attach, stays black, giving it that classic tuxedo look.

Now I'm assembling the full build script -- setting up the spine as a chain of joints from hips to neck, sweeping a body silhouette along it with the black-and-white coat paint, then attaching a head sphere at the top of the neck with its own paint and a beak made from joint-mounted parts. I'm adding wing chains on each side as flipper shapes tapering from shoulder to hand, and foot and tail details extruded from outline shapes and attached near the hip joint. Writing build script...
